title: Finance U4·W1 — Job Cost Architecture: Cost Codes, Burden, Committed Cost & the Sub-Ledger Tie
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the applied track starts here

Units 1 through 3 built the corporate-finance spine: time value, valuation, cost of capital, capital budgeting, forecasting. Units 4 through 7 take that spine and drive it through a contractor’s general ledger. Everything here is CMA Part 1 content wearing work clothes. Job costing is Part 1-D Cost Management. WIP and revenue are Part 1-A External Financial Reporting. Close and cutoff controls are Part 1-E Internal Controls. Budgets, draw schedules and overhead absorption are Part 1-B Planning, Budgeting and Forecasting. A rep on a construction workpaper is not a detour from the exam — it is the same skill, tagged the same way, and it moves the same readiness number.

All examples use fictional companies: Meridian Building Group LLC (homebuilding and general contracting), Riverton Partners LLC (land development), and Northstar Services LLC (labor and equipment). Every dollar figure in this unit is invented.

The job is the cost object

In manufacturing, the cost object is a batch or a process. In construction it is the job — a contract, a lot, a building, or a phase — and the accounting system is a textbook job-order costing system. Every dollar of cost must answer three questions before it posts: which job, which cost code, and which cost type. Miss any one and the cost lands somewhere that cannot be analyzed.

  • Job number — the contract or lot. This is the profit-center dimension.
  • Cost code — the scope of work, usually a division-and-item code (03-300 concrete, 06-100 rough framing, 15-400 plumbing). This is the budget-comparison dimension.
  • Cost type — L labor, M material, S subcontract, E equipment, O other. This is the behavior dimension, and it is what lets you tell an overrun caused by hours from one caused by price.

The three together form the cost-code key. A budget is loaded at this key, actuals post at this key, and every variance report is a join on this key. If field staff can post to a job without a cost code, the system will happily accumulate an unanalyzable pile.

Direct, indirect and the burden calculation

Direct costs trace to one job: the framing crew’s hours, the lumber package, the plumbing subcontract. Indirect construction costs benefit many jobs — superintendents, trucks, small tools, jobsite trailers, project managers — and are absorbed to jobs through a rate (Unit 7 Week 4 builds that rate and its variances). General and administrative costs — the office, the controller, the owner’s salary — are period costs and never touch a job.

Self-performed labor is the trap inside the trap, because the wage is only part of the cost. Burden must be applied at the moment payroll posts to the job, not annually in an adjusting entry. Meridian’s burden build:

Meridian Building Group — labor burden rate build
ComponentRate on gross wages
Employer FICA7.65%
FUTA and SUTA1.85%
Workers’ compensation11.50%
General liability (payroll-rated)2.00%
Health and retirement benefits5.00%
Paid time off2.00%
Total burden rate30.00%

On Job 2418 (Willow Bend custom residence) the framing crew earned $60,000 of gross wages. Burden = $60,000 × 30.00% = $18,000, so the job carries $78,000 of burdened framing labor, not $60,000. A contractor who bids using unburdened labor bids 23.1% light on every self-perform line ($18,000 ÷ $78,000), and the gap shows up later as gross-profit fade with no identifiable cause.

The job cost ledger versus the general ledger

The job cost system is a sub-ledger. The general ledger holds one or a few control accounts — work in process, cost of revenue — and the sub-ledger holds the detail by job and cost code. The unbreakable rule is the same one that governs accounts payable and fixed assets: the sub-ledger must foot to the control account, every period, to the penny.

Job 2418 — inception-to-date job cost ledger at September 30
Cost codeTypeInception-to-date cost
03-300 ConcreteS$42,500
06-100 Rough framing (burdened labor)L$78,000
06-200 Framing materialM$61,400
15-400 PlumbingS$29,750
16-100 ElectricalS$24,300
Total job cost ledger$235,950

The GL work-in-process account for Job 2418 reads $238,700. The difference is $2,750, and there is exactly one acceptable response: find it. Here the cause was a plumbing invoice posted directly to the WIP account with a job number but no cost code, so it hit the GL and never reached the sub-ledger. The fix is not a plug entry; it is re-coding the invoice and then turning off the ability to post to WIP without a cost code. A reconciling item you cannot name is an error you have not found yet.

The trap: an “ending balance” column that is not cumulative

Job cost reports are exported constantly, and the column headings lie more often than you would believe. Meridian’s September export carries a column labeled Ending Balance. It is not an inception-to-date balance. It is period activity — costs posted in September only. For Job 2418 that column totals $54,050 (plumbing $29,750 plus electrical $24,300), while the true inception-to-date figure is $235,950.

Now watch what that does downstream. Against a total budget of $295,000:

  • Correct percent complete = $235,950 ÷ $295,000 = 79.98%.
  • Percent complete using the mislabeled column = $54,050 ÷ $295,000 = 18.32%.

A job that is four-fifths built reports as barely started, earned revenue collapses, and the WIP schedule swings by more than sixty points of completion on a single job. The defense is procedural, not clever: before any export becomes an input to a schedule, foot it and tie it. Sum the column and compare it to the GL control account. $54,050 does not equal $238,700, so the column is not what its heading claims, and you find that out in ten seconds instead of at the audit.

Committed cost — the number that is not in the ledger

The job cost ledger is history. The forecast needs committed cost: signed subcontracts and issued purchase orders that are not yet invoiced. Job 2418 carries $41,300 of open commitments, so:

  • Projected cost at completion = $235,950 incurred + $41,300 committed = $277,250.
  • Versus budget $295,000, that is $17,750 favorable — if nothing else is missing.

The discipline is asking what is missing. Committed cost only covers scope that has been bought out. Unbought scope carries no commitment and therefore no visibility, which is why the cost-at-completion estimate must always be built as incurred + committed + estimate of unbought scope. Unit 4 Week 4 builds that estimate to complete properly.

Data flow: where cost enters the system

Costs reach a job through five doors, and each door needs a control: payroll (time coded by job and cost code, then burdened), accounts payable (invoice matched to a subcontract or purchase order, coded on entry), subcontract pay applications (schedule-of-values based, with retention withheld), equipment and internal charges (an hourly or daily rate charged to the job and credited to the equipment pool), and journal entries (reclasses and accruals). Any door that can bypass coding is a hole in the job cost system. The most common hole is the credit-card feed that posts to an expense account with no job dimension at all.

A second architectural point matters for reporting: the job cost system and the general ledger are often different applications, with different charts of accounts and different period-close mechanics. That is normal and workable, but it makes the crosswalk a formal deliverable — a mapping from every job cost account to a GL account, maintained under change control, tested at every close. When someone adds a cost code and forgets the crosswalk, the cost posts to the job and disappears from the GL, or vice versa, and the difference shows up as an unexplained sub-ledger break next month.

Reading a job cost report like a controller

A job cost report has four columns that matter and one habit that separates a controller from a bookkeeper. The columns are original budget, approved revisions, cost to date, and cost at completion. The habit is reading them by cost code, not in total, because totals hide offsetting errors. On Job 2418 the concrete code came in $4,200 under and the plumbing code $6,900 over; in total the job looks $2,700 over, which is a number nobody can act on. Broken out, one is a buyout win to bank and the other is a scope question to answer before the same subcontractor bids the next four houses.

Three questions get asked on every line that moves. Is it price or quantity? A material line that grew because lumber prices rose is a market event; one that grew because the takeoff was short is an estimating defect that will repeat on every similar house. Is it in scope or out? Out-of-scope work performed without an executed change order is cost with no matching revenue, and it converts directly into gross-profit fade (Unit 4 Week 4). Is the budget still right? A budget that has never been revised on a job that has been running six months is not a control — it is a decoration.

Finally, the report has to be read against the schedule. Cost to date of 79.98% on a house the superintendent says is at drywall is coherent. Cost to date of 79.98% on a house still at foundation means either the costs are miscoded to the wrong job or the budget is badly wrong, and both are findable in an afternoon. The cheapest reconciliation in construction accounting is walking the job with the report in your hand.

CMA bridge

Everything above is Part 1-D Cost Management: job-order costing, direct versus indirect classification, cost-object definition, and the sub-ledger-to-control-account relationship. The burden rate is a predetermined overhead rate applied to a cost driver. The sub-ledger tie is the same reconciliation logic Part 1-E tests as a control activity. Do the job cost rep on a Tuesday and you have done the exam rep.

Practice and recap

  1. Code every cost to job + cost code + cost type. A cost with only a job number is an unanalyzable cost.
  2. Burden self-perform labor at the moment payroll posts: $60,000 wages × 30.00% = $18,000 burden = $78,000 burdened.
  3. Foot the job cost sub-ledger to the GL control account every close. $235,950 versus $238,700 is a $2,750 error to be named, not plugged.
  4. Never trust a column heading. An “Ending Balance” column that is period activity turned 79.98% complete into 18.32% complete.
  5. Forecast with incurred + committed + unbought: $235,950 + $41,300 = $277,250 against a $295,000 budget.

Recap: construction accounting is job-order costing with a sub-ledger, and the controller’s job is to keep the coding key intact, the burden applied, the sub-ledger tied to the control account to the penny, and every exported column footed before it feeds a schedule — because a mislabeled export column is a bigger threat to reported gross profit than any estimating error.

flashcards.back: Job number + cost code + cost type (L/M/S/E/O). Budgets load at this key, actuals post at this key, and every variance report joins on it. A cost with only a job number cannot be analyzed.
Direct = traces to one job. Indirect construction = supers, trucks, small tools, PMs — absorbed to jobs via a rate. G&A = office/period cost, never touches a job.
FICA 7.65% + FUTA/SUTA 1.85% + workers' comp 11.50% + GL insurance 2.00% + benefits 5.00% + PTO 2.00% = 30.00% of gross wages.
$60,000 gross framing wages × 30.00% = $18,000 burden → $78,000 burdened labor on the job. Bidding unburdened understates the labor line by $18,000 ÷ $78,000 = 23.1%.
The job cost sub-ledger must foot to the GL control account (WIP / cost of revenue) to the penny every period. Job 2418: ledger $235,950 vs GL $238,700 = $2,750 to be NAMED, not plugged.

An export column labeled Ending Balance may be PERIOD activity. Job 2418: $54,050 (period) vs $235,950 (ITD). % complete on a $295,000 budget: 18.32% (wrong) vs 79.98% (right). Foot the export and tie it to the GL first.
Signed subcontracts and issued POs not yet invoiced. Job 2418: $235,950 incurred + $41,300 committed = $277,250 projected vs $295,000 budget = $17,750 favorable — only if all scope is bought out.
Incurred + committed + estimate of UNBOUGHT scope. Committed cost only covers bought-out work, so a projection using incurred + committed alone silently omits everything not yet awarded.

questions.q: Job 2418 has $60,000 of gross framing wages and Meridian's burden rate is 30.00%. What burdened labor cost should post to the job?
questions.explain: $60,000 × 30.00% = $18,000 burden; $60,000 + $18,000 = $78,000. Burden is applied when payroll posts, not in a year-end entry.

questions.q: The Job 2418 cost sub-ledger totals $235,950 and the GL WIP control account reads $238,700. The correct response is to:
choices: Post a $2,750 plug to the sub-ledger
questions.explain: A reconciling item you cannot name is an unfound error. Here it was an invoice posted to WIP with a job number but no cost code — fix the coding and close the control gap.

questions.q: An export column labeled 'Ending Balance' actually contains September activity of $54,050 for Job 2418, whose inception-to-date cost is $235,950. Against a $295,000 budget, using the mislabeled column reports percent complete as:
questions.explain: $54,050 ÷ $295,000 = 18.32%; $235,950 ÷ $295,000 = 79.98%. Foot every export and tie it to the GL before it feeds a schedule.

questions.q: Job 2418 has incurred $235,950 and holds $41,300 of open subcontracts and POs. Projected cost at completion versus a $295,000 budget is:
questions.explain: $235,950 + $41,300 = $277,250; $295,000 − $277,250 = $17,750 favorable, valid only if all remaining scope is bought out.

questions.q: Which cost is an INDIRECT construction cost absorbed to jobs by a rate, rather than a direct cost or G&A?
choices: A jobsite superintendent covering four active jobs
questions.explain: A superintendent benefits many jobs — indirect construction overhead, absorbed via a rate. Subcontracts and material trace directly; the controller is G&A.

questions.q: Why must the cost TYPE (L/M/S/E/O) be captured in addition to the job and cost code?
choices: It separates an overrun caused by hours from one caused by price
It determines the customer's retainage percentage
It sets the general ledger account for cash
It is required to file the contract
questions.explain: Cost type is the behavior dimension — it lets you decompose a variance into labor-hour, material-price and subcontract-buyout causes.

questions.q: A company credit-card feed posts fuel and small tools to an expense account with no job dimension. The primary consequence is:
choices: Job cost is understated and the sub-ledger no longer explains the control account
questions.explain: Any door into the ledger that bypasses job coding creates cost that exists in the GL but not in the job cost system — the classic sub-ledger-to-control break.
